newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African cities get more clout over housing.
newsitem.headline: S.African cities get more clout over housing.

text.p: South Africa's cities will be given greater control of national housing schemes in a bid to speed up construction, Housing Minister Sankie Mthembi-Mahanyele said on Tuesday.

She told parliament that a bill on housing would soon be presented which would among other things "empower provincial and local government to administer national housing programmes for the first time."
"It makes sense to devolve to local government those housing matters which would most effectively be administered locally," she said.

"Municipalities will now be able to offer new homeowners the best value for money," she said, adding that she expected that initially only the major cities would have the facilities and expertise to take part in the process.

Local authorities would have to apply for accreditation to administer the housing subsidy scheme and would have to demonstrate that they could properly account for funds with which they were entrusted.
The minister said a recent probe into the speed of housing delivery had found that lack of participation by local authorities was one of the major constraints.

"The administration of the housing subsidy scheme by local government bodies will ensure that centres for the application of subsidies and advice on housing matters are readily accessible to potential beneficiaries," Mthembi-Mahanyele said.

The minister said last month her ministry had so far approved 555,000 housing subsidies, showing the government was still on track to deliver on its promise to build one million houses during its first five years in office.
More than seven million South Africans live in informal shanties and the official housing backlog tops two million units.

The government conceded soon after coming into power that it could not physically build and deliver a million houses and, instead, implemented a subsidy scheme offering up to 15,000 rand to the poorest families.
About half the subsidy goes towards the cost of serviced plots and the rest is available for basic structures. Some projects include private-sector loans to bolster the subsidies.
